Yes. By game three, the opening line was completely solved: park the crank two pins from your mill, bridge the gap on turn one with a single low gear, and bank two points for the solo clockwise bonus. After that, every turn reduced to a binary check: does this gear flip my parity or close an odd loop? In two-player, it collapsed further into a pass-spiral where both sides just extended safe leaf gears or passed to trigger the "no gear placed" end condition, leaving the final-grind tiebreaker to decide the match. The cost to the game is severe: the stated tension of managing a shared, interlocking mesh network evaporates the moment the opening parity trick is known, leaving only attrition, bind-avoidance, and end-condition exploitation. A game that survives three sessions of actively trying to kill its own opening line deserves credit, but Millbind does not. It becomes a rote exercise in avoiding triangles and waiting for the opponent to run out of legal moves.

Did this game get smaller? Yes, drastically.

What I know now: Millbind is not a spatial placement game; it is a parity lock. The crank’s position dictates power, so building chains away from it is pointless because the next start player simply moves the crank elsewhere. The winning line is a three-turn script: place your mill, move the crank to a yard pin adjacent to yours, place a single gear to bridge them (creating a one-gear odd chain for a clockwise turn and solo bonus), then pass. Gear tiers only matter to avoid binding triangles, not for long-term strategy.

What it cost: The middle and end games evaporate. Once the crank is parked and bridged, the rest of the round is just passing or making cosmetic fills. The solo bonus rule makes deep chain-building obsolete, turning a stated 35-minute supply management puzzle into a solved opening sequence. If both players know the line, the game ends before the gear pile matters.

Yes. After game one I believed mill placement and crank racing were the main levers; now I know the real constraint is lattice parity. Whoever anchors an inner pin on turn one dictates odd/even paths for everyone else, collapsing the opening from a spatial puzzle into a parity race. It cost the game its early branching: turns two through six are now just safe extensions of a known template, and the middlegame devolves into reactive tandem placements or forced passes because any new gear risks an odd-cycle bind. The bind test is so unforgiving that “build a network” became “don’t close a triangle,” turning a spatial engine into a counting exercise. I’m no longer guessing on turn four, but the discovery phase is over.

Yes. After game one I thought the inner ring was a contest; it is a script. Mill on (0,3), then low on (1,1) and high on (0,1) is a forced opening that guarantees isolation and an odd-parity path. The decision space collapsed entirely to crank rerouting and late-game tandem bridges.

Cost: The supply pile becomes a parking lot. Once parity is set, the remaining turns are mechanical bind-tests where placing anything that closes a triangle wastes the action and placing anything on an empty rim pin changes nothing. Thinking stopped mattering by round four.

Finding: Millbind is not about meshing gears; it is about counting parity steps to your mill and moving the crank to keep that count odd. Everything else is table management.
